summaries.summary: RNNs in SMT reduce memory use to about 5%, jointly optimize modules, but require heavy corpora, harming translation involving morphologically rich languages.
MT efficiency depends on parallel corpus availability and size and syntactic divergence, with agglutinative morphologically rich languages differing from fusional languages like English.
Agglutination creates many Tamil inflectional forms, at least 30,000 per verb and about 5,000 per noun, hiding meanings and increasing MT complexity.
Tamil translation is difficult because parallel corpus availability is very scarce and most English–Tamil MT corpora were manually created and unavailable online.
Tamil pronunciation-based suffix characters, unique for each consonant, degrade MT because words with different suffixes are treated as different words.
Tamil has written and spoken forms, creating two corpus versions and increasing vocabulary, as seen between Bible sentences and movie subtitles.
Building an English–Tamil neural MT system requires a trade-off between domain specificity and size of the corpus.
The experiment corpus combined EnTam v2, TDIL tourism data, and AU-KBC Tamil novels and short stories, totaling 197,792 sentences.
A self-collected monolingual Tamil corpus of 567,772 sentences supported word2vec embeddings and a phrase-based SMT language model, with UTF-8 standardization and cleaning.
Source and target word embeddings initialize model vectors, and the word2vec skip gram model optimizes vectors using average log probability of context words.
The formulation defines k, corpus words, and hierarchical softmax probability, while negative sampling and subsampling of frequent words are not used.
A monolingual corpus of 569,772 Tamil sentences was used to create semantically meaningful word embeddings with richer context than bilingual target-side sentences.
The word2vec model used vector size 100, window size 5, 7 worker threads, batch size 50 words, negative sampling 1, and gensim.
The Bahdanau et al. model uses a bidirectional LSTM encoder and attention-based decoder with weighted encoder outputs, previous hidden output, and previously decoded word.
Neural Machine Translation computes target sentence probability word by word, with basic and attention-based decoders using different log probability formulations.
The attention formulation defines target sentence length, target and source sentences, encoder output vector, and attention vector enabling selective source sentence lookup.
The decoder LSTM computes a displayed equation.
Decoder probability depends on previous output, current hidden layer vector, and attention context vector, which is a weighted sum over sentence outputs.
The context vector uses source tokens, encoder hidden values, and an alignment parameter from a feed forward neural network trained jointly with the model.
Softmax alignment uses decoder hidden state and encoder annotation, with concatenated forward and reverse encoder hidden parameters computing attention weights for overall sentence context.
Global attention is preferred over local attention because English–Tamil structural discordance and morphological and structural variations make local lookup inefficient.
The No Peepholes (NP) LSTM variant from Greff et al. greff2015lstm is used, with gated cell and hidden vectors preventing vanishing gradients.
The decoder uses equations 7 through 11, while the encoder uses a bidirectional RNN LSTM with forward and reverse hidden components.
Morphological segmentation uses a semi-supervised extension of a generative probabilistic model maximizing MAP probability of prefix,root,postfix recursive word splits.
The prior is estimated using the Minimum Description Length(MDL) principle, and the likelihood is estimated with a displayed equation.
The likelihood equation refers to intermediate analyses and the morpheme of a word.
An extension to the Viterbi algorithm performs decoding, with extra parameters and a cost function addressing over-segmentation and under-segmentation.
The cost function includes likelihoods for the cost function, annotated dataset contribution, and labeled data, with parameters controlling segment size and corpus discrepancies.
The Python extension to morfessor 2.0 performed segmentation using Tamil annotation data from Anoop Kunchukkutan in the Indic NLP Library.
English to Tamil translation used an RNN LSTM Bi-directional encoder attention decoder architecture, with phrase based SMT, Factored SMT reference, and 569,772 monolingual Tamil sentences.
Bucketing minimized PAD tokens around the 10–20 words region, with RNNMorph target sentence bucket counts uniformly increased by 5.
RNNSearch vocabularies were restricted to 60,000 out of 67,768 English and 150,000 out of 340,325 Tamil words, while RNNMorph used 67,768 English and 41,906 Tamil words.
The model used SGD with sampled softmax loss of 512 per sample, learning rate 1.0, decay 0.5, gradient clipping global norm 5.0, and Tensorflow seq2seq.
Evaluation used BLEU modified 1-gram, 2-gram, 3-gram and 4-gram precision values and human metrics of adequacy, fluency and relative ranking values.
The BLEU scores obtained using the various models are tabulated in Table TABREF25.
BLEU computes micro-averaged unigram, bigram, trigram and BLEU-4 precision, showing phrase-based SMT inferior to RNNSearch and slight gains from word2vec vectors.
Morphological segmentation improved BLEU precision in RNNMorph, but increased word units per sentence may make the numeric increase inefficiently describe performance.
Human evaluation used 50 native annotators, about 100 randomized test sentences, 5-point adequacy and fluency scales, ranking, and intra-annotator values.
The human evaluation Kappa co-efficient results are calculated with respect to a displayed equation.
Ranking Kappa co-efficient was 0.573 for RNNMorph and 0.410 for RNNSearch+Word2Vec, implying annotators found RNNMorph produced better results.
Manual learning rate decay followed perplexity stagnation, and RNNMorph saturated earlier as segmentation reduced Tamil vocabulary from 340,325 words to 41,906 morphs.
Sampled SoftMax loss accommodated a large target vocabulary, and RNNMorph showed consistently better perplexity values than RNNSearch + Word2Vec with 4 hidden layers.
Attention vector comparisons show reduced vocabulary improves source lookup, while RNNSearch with Word2Vec attends to EOS mid-sentence due to limited vocabulary coverage.
Tamil morphological richness creates a large target vocabulary, but segmentation decreased it from 340,325 to 41,906, reducing unknown tokens and splitting roots and inflections.
RNNMorph translations sometimes repeat phrases, possibly due to longer morph sequences, greater LSTM and attention demands, and semi-supervised segmentation errors.
RNNSearch + Word2Vec and Morph2Vec outputs show morphological segmentation improves grammatical soundness, with most Morph2Vec sentences lacking UNK tokens.
Related English–Tamil MT work includes MAT, EBMT with 700000 sentences, rule based systems, HMM alignment, hybrid approaches, SMT, and morphological processing techniques.
RNN Encoder Decoder models performed well for similar grammatical structures, with Cho et al SecondOneByCho and Sutskever et al. sutskever2014sequence limited by static context vectors.
Bahdanau et al. Bahdanau2014 introduced variable length word vectors and attention, later analysed by Luong et al. luong2015effective using global and local attention and AER scores.
Morphological segmentation improves translation for morphologically rich languages and should be applied to both languages when their agglutination schemes differ.
Morphological segmentation increases average sentence lengths and model complexity, but attention models and agglutination-related shorter Tamil sentences remain relevant.
The implemented model lacks target side morphological agglutination, so an end-to-end system for morphologically rich languages requires a morphological generator.
A better corpus and better GPU could enhance generalization, hidden layer sizes, batch sizes, and possibly learning scope and accuracy.
Rocktaschel et al. rocktaschel2015reasoning's encoder–decoder architecture for Natural Language Inference (NLI) may be used for Machine Translation.
The author thanks Dr. M. Anand Kumar of Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham and Dr. Arvindan of SSN College Of Engineering for support, guidance, inputs and suggestions.
